think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 15-year-old boy from Chongqing presents with prolonged high fevers spiking to 41°C, cytopenias, splenomegaly (thickness 6.6 cm), hepatic transaminitis, marked hyperferritinemia (>2000 ng/mL), hypertriglyceridemia, and elevated LDH, along with positive direct Coombs and autoimmune antibodies (ANA, RF, anti-Jo-1). This clinical and biochemical picture strongly mimics secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), autoimmune disease, or hematologic malignancy, failing empiric cephalosporin antibiotics and corticosteroids. The clinical tension centers on identifying an endemic protozoan parasite causing reticuloendothelial hyperactivation and secondary autoantibody production.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint concludes following emergency triage, physical examination demonstrating splenomegaly, initial laboratory testing (CBC, liver function, ferritin, LDH, triglycerides, autoantibodies, negative blood cultures), and imaging (chest CT, abdominal ultrasound), strictly prior to blood mNGS pathogen identification, CDC rK39 antibody results, and targeted treatment with sodium stibogluconate.
3. Differential Distinctions: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) was considered given fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, and hypertriglyceridemia, but HLH was driven by an occult parasitic infection rather than primary or malignant HLH. Systemic autoimmune disease was suspected due to positive ANA, RF, anti-Jo-1, and positive direct Coombs test, but these represented polyclonal B-cell activation from visceral leishmaniasis. Molecular mNGS and rK39 antibody testing confirmed visceral leishmaniasis.
case_prompt:
A 15-year-old male student residing in Chongqing presents to the emergency fever clinic with a persistent febrile illness and cough of several weeks' duration. His illness began with low-grade fever fluctuating between 37°C and 38°C, fatigue, chills, dry cough, and pharyngeal discomfort following a presumed viral upper respiratory illness. Over the preceding month, his symptoms escalated into high-grade daily fevers peaking at 41°C, partially responsive to oral antipyretics. At an outside hospital, initial investigations revealed cytopenias (white blood cell count 3.3 x 10^9/L, hemoglobin 85 g/L, platelet count 87 x 10^9/L), hyperferritinemia exceeding 2,000 ng/mL, procalcitonin of 4.14 ng/mL, and an initial bone marrow aspirate demonstrating active trilineage hyperplasia with 9.5% lymphocytes. Broad-spectrum empiric therapy with cefoperazone-sulbactam yielded no clinical improvement, prompting referral.

On presentation, his temperature is 37.1°C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute, and blood pressure 110/72 mmHg. Physical examination of the abdomen reveals marked splenomegaly.

Emergency laboratory testing reveals a white blood cell count of 4.68 x 10^9/L, hemoglobin 100 g/L, and red blood cell count 3.65 x 10^12/L. Biochemical evaluation demonstrates alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 204 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 176 IU/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 153 IU/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 889 IU/L, serum triglycerides 2.29 mmol/L, serum ferritin >2,000 ng/mL, procalcitonin 2.11 ng/mL, C-reactive protein 53.5 mg/L, and interleukin-6 31.58 pg/mL. A direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is positive (++). Autoimmune screening reveals an antinuclear antibody (ANA) titer of 1:100, positive anti-Jo-1 antibody, and rheumatoid factor of 207 IU/mL. Screening tests for HIV, syphilis, and SARS-CoV-2 are negative. Blood cultures show no bacterial growth after five days.

Chest CT shows no acute parenchymal abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasonography confirms marked splenomegaly with an intercostal spleen thickness of approximately 6.6 cm.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Secondary Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) / Macrophage Activation Syndrome
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the presence of prolonged high fevers, splenomegaly, cytopenias, marked hyperferritinemia (>2000 ng/mL), hypertriglyceridemia, and elevated LDH; however, rather than idiopathic or malignant HLH, the hyperinflammatory state was triggered by an occult intracellular protozoan infection.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Ferritin: >2,000 ng/ml; PCT: 2.11 ng/ml; CRP: 53.5 mg/L, IL-6 31.58 pg/ml... Abdominal ultrasound showed that the spleen thickness was ~6.6 cm intercostal, suggesting splenomegaly... The diagnosis was considered to be: (1) FUO:sepsis with hematological disease? Do not exclude the possibility of parasitic diseases? Hemophilic cell syndrome? Lymphoma? Autoimmune disease?

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given positive direct Coombs test, ANA (1:100), anti-Jo-1 antibody, and elevated rheumatoid factor; however, these represented nonspecific polyclonal B-cell activation secondary to reticuloendothelial infection, and empiric dexamethasone failed to control the fever.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Coombs' test (direct anti-human globulin test): positive, ++. Autoimmune antibody: ANA + 1:100; Anti-jo-1 antibody +; RF 207 IU/ml... dexamethasone administered to reduce the fever; however, the patient showed no significant relief of fever.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Plasma metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) identified Leishmania infantum on day 4, and CDC rK39 antibody testing confirmed visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar); intravenous sodium stibogluconate (SSG) led to prompt defervescence within 72 hours, spleen retraction to 4.5 cm, and normalization of liver function and hematology.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: On the fourth day, the mNGS test results of the patient showed Leishmania infantum (Figure 4). CDC was contacted for rK39 antibody test, and the antibody was detected to be positive on the seventh day, which is in accordance with the criteria for clinically diagnosed cases. The anti-kala-azar treatment was started and sodium stibogluconate was administered.

editor_comments: Distilled strictly per Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Zero pathogen spoilers in the admission prompt; details the diagnostic challenge between HLH, autoimmune connective tissue disease, and visceral leishmaniasis.
